# PROBLEM 1: 


### 1.1 Evaluating data set
```{r echo=TRUE}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
```

The dataset is structurally tidy and has `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns, with one row per station per day, from `r n_distinct(pull(ny_noaa, id))` NY weather stations between `r min(pull(ny_noaa, date))` and `r max(pull(ny_noaa, date))`. Key variables are precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), and daily max/min temperature (`tmax`, `tmin`). Missing data is a substantial issue, particularly for temperature: `tmax` is
missing in about `r round(100 * mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax))))`% of rows, largely because many stations do not record temperature, so temperature summaries reflect only a subset of stations. This could result in average values that are not representative of the true daily maximum temperature. The same issue applied to `tmin`. The rest of the variables also have missing values, although to lesser degree.  

### 1.2 Data cleaning

```{r echo=TRUE}

ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-", convert = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    month = month.name[month] |> factor(levels = month.name),
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )

ny_noaa_df
```

The cleaned data now has the corresponding variables for year, month, and day, as well as the correct units for precipitation and temperature (tenths of mm and degress of C, respectively). I reorganized

###### 1.2a Most commonly observed values of snowfall

```{r}
ny_noaa_df |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(6) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The most commonly observed values for snowfall is 0 (2,008,508), followed by NA, 25, 13, 51,  and 76. This indicates that, overall, it does not snow on most days. 

### 1.3 Two-panel plot: Mean tmax per year 

```{r}

mean_tmax_vs_year_plot =
ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c("January", "July")) |>
  drop_na(tmax) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_point( alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average max temperature by station, January vs July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean daily max temperature (°C)"
  )

mean_tmax_vs_year_plot
```

Average maximum temperatures are much higher in July (station means mostly between 20 and 33 °C) than in January (mostly between -10 and 10 °C). January is also more variable, both across stations within a year and from year to year. Within each month, stations tend to move together, meaning that in a cold year, such as January 1994 or 2004, nearly all stations are colder than usual, which suggests statewide weather patterns rather than station-specific effects. There is no clear long-term trend in either month over the 30 years.

There are several outliers. In January, individual stations were noticeably colder than the rest of the state in 1982 (-13 °C), 1993, and 2005, while in 2004 a few stations were much warmer than the rest (7 to 10 °C when most were below 0 °C). In July, the outliers are mostly on the cold side: one station averaged 14 °C in 1988, and another averaged 19 °C in 1984, when the other stations ranged up to about 29 °C.

### 1.4a Two-panel plot: tmax vs tmin 

```{r}

tmax_tmin_plot =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmin, tmax) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Max vs min temperature",
    x = "Minimum daily temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum daily temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Number of days"
  ) +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"))

tmax_tmin_plot 
```

The plot shows hexagons, each of which represents the number of station-days with that combination of minimum and maximum temperature, with lighter colors indicating more days. The plot shows a positive association between the two, meaning that days with higher minimum temperatures also tend to have higher maximum temperatures, forming an ascending diagonal band. Observations are concentrated in two areas, one around a minimum of 12–15 °C and a maximum of 24–27 °C (typical summer days), and one around a minimum of -3 °C and a maximum of 3 °C (typical winter days). There are a few suspicious values, likely resulting from recording error. For example, some days have maximum and minimum temperatures of 60 °C, and some have a minimum temperature higher than the maximum. 


### 1.4b Two-panel plot: Snowfall per year

```{r}

snow_plot =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 13, 25, 51, 76, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall between 0 and 100 mm, by year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

snow_plot
```

The plot shows the distribution of snowfall values between 0 and 100 mm for each year, with year treated as a categorical variable and the density curves stacked on top of each other from 1981 to 2010. The distributions look very similar from year to year. Rather than being smooth, each ridge has distinct peaks, the largest at around 13 and 25 mm, with smaller peaks at around 51 and 76 mm.
